cards.goal: Investors and analysts understand the period's performance and outlook accurately and trust management's candour.

structure.does: Company, period and the one or two headline numbers with their change
Revenue, EBITDA and margin, profit, the key operating metric, each against the prior period
MD or CEO on what drove the result and what comes next: one specific point, no adjectives
By segment or geography: numbers, drivers, one-offs explained
What management expects and on what assumptions, or an explicit 'no guidance'
Capex, order wins, board decisions already disclosed to the exchange
Boilerplate, forward-looking-statements caution, IR contact
Reported numbers and the reconciliation of any adjusted metric

length.note: Earnings releases run about 600-1,200 words plus tables; shareholder letters run longer; IR web pages 150-400 words each.

checklist: Does the headline give the period and the headline numbers with their change?
Is every figure compared with a stated prior period (YoY or QoQ)?
Are adjusted metrics reconciled to reported numbers?
Is bad news (decline, write-off, delay) stated as plainly as good news, with its cause?
Does the management quote say something specific rather than adjectives?
Is there a forward-looking-statements caution wherever outlook is discussed?
Do all numbers match the board-approved results filed with the exchange?
Is the copy scheduled to go out only after, or with, the exchange filing?
Is one unit system used throughout (e.g. Rs crore with consistent decimals)?
pitfalls: Selective emphasis (leading with the one segment that grew while consolidated revenue fell): lead with consolidated numbers, then segments.
Changing a metric's definition between quarters without saying so: disclose the change and restate the prior period.
Last quarter's quote with the numbers swapped: analysts read every quarter; say what is new.
Drafting from unfinished numbers: use placeholders and run a final number check against the filed results before release.
cards.exemplar_brief: Q2 FY27 earnings press release for an NSE-listed Ahmedabad specialty-chemicals company; supplied numbers: revenue Rs 642 crore (+11% YoY), EBITDA margin 17.8% (down 120 basis points on raw-material costs), PAT Rs 71 crore (+4%), commissioning of the new Dahej plant delayed by one quarter; audience: analysts and institutional and retail investors; English; 700-1,000 words plus a table placeholder; must include a forward-looking-statements caution; goal: an accurate understanding of the margin dip and the delay.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Headline leads with consolidated numbers and the bad news (margin -120 bps, Dahej delay), release-after-filing line, highlights vs Q2 FY26, plain cause for the margin dip, PAT-slower-than-revenue explained, no-adjective quote, outlook choice, full forward-looking caution, table with reconciliation row. Weak spots: EBITDA in rupees (~Rs 114 crore = 642 x 17.8%) and prior-year revenue/PAT (~Rs 578 / ~Rs 68 crore) are derivable but left blank; the MD quote's one specific point is a placeholder, so the quote just restates the numbers.

cards.name: Investor update
cards.summary: A regular monthly or quarterly note from a founder to existing investors: headline metrics against last period and plan, highlights, lowlights, priorities for the next period and specific asks. Good updates use the same structure every time, put bad news early and plainly, and make each ask specific enough that an investor can act on it in one reply.
use_for: Monthly or quarterly updates to angels and VCs
avoid: Writing only when news is good: irregular updates read as hiding something; keep the same cadence and format in bad months.
Burying the miss: lowlights go near the top, with the cause and what you are doing about it.
Vague asks ('any intros would help'): name the company, role or person type ('Intro to the procurement head at a quick-commerce company').
Listed-company reporting is genre:investor_relations_copy; a deck for new investors is genre:investor_pitch_deck.
buyers: Founder's office and chiefs of staff
cards.value_why: Low: founders write these themselves; little external paid demand.
cards.goal: Investors understand where the company stands in two minutes and act on at least one ask.

structure.does: Company, period and the one-line headline ('Sept 2026: MRR Rs 18.4L (+6%), runway 13 months')
Headline metric, biggest win, biggest problem
The same 5-8 metrics every time: this period, last period, plan, change; cash and runway
2-4 wins, each with a number
1-3 misses or risks, the cause and the response
3 priorities with measurable targets
1-3 specific asks (intros, hires, advice) with context
One line of thanks, optionally naming an investor who helped

length.note: Monthly updates stay short (around 300-500 words); quarterly ones add narrative and board-level detail.

checklist: Does the subject line carry the period and the headline metric?
Is there a 3-bullet TL;DR at the top?
Are the same metrics reported as last time, with last period and plan side by side?
Are cash and runway stated?
Is at least one lowlight stated plainly with cause and response?
Are next-period priorities measurable?
Is every ask specific enough to act on in one reply?
Is it under about 700 words?
pitfalls: Changing which metrics are shown when they look bad: investors compare with last month; keep the set and explain the drop.
Narrative without numbers ('great month, strong momentum'): every highlight gets a figure.
Customer names or deal terms in an email that may be forwarded: anonymise or mark the update confidential.
Hiding a short runway: say how many months remain and the plan; investors can't help with what they don't know.
cards.exemplar_brief: September 2026 monthly investor update from the founder of a Bengaluru B2B SaaS for clinic appointment booking to 9 angels and 1 seed fund; supplied: MRR Rs 18.4 lakh (+6% month on month against a +10% plan), churn up from 2.1% to 3.4% after a pricing change, 2 hospital-chain pilots signed, cash Rs 2.6 crore, runway 13 months; asks: an intro to a hospital-chain CIO and referrals for a senior sales hire; English; 300-500 words.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Subject with period and headline metrics, 3-bullet TL;DR with the problem stated plainly, metrics table with derived Aug/plan figures labelled as derived, cash/runway/implied burn, lowlight with cause and response, measurable priorities, two one-reply asks. Writer slip: 'This is why MRR missed plan by about Rs 0.7 lakh' over-attributes; 1.3 points of extra churn on ~Rs 17.4 lakh MRR is ~Rs 0.23 lakh, so churn explains about a third of the miss. Investors will check that arithmetic.

cards.name: IVR / on-hold message script
cards.summary: The words callers hear in a phone system: welcome greeting, language choice, menu options, hold-queue messages and after-hours greeting. Good IVR copy is written for the ear: short prompts, few options with the most-used first, one fixed pattern for every option, a repeat option, honest wait information with a call-back offer, and one consistent voice.
use_for: Business IVR menus (banks, hospitals, D2C support, helplines)
avoid: Long menus: Exotel's guidance is 4-5 options per menu and no more than three menu levels, with the most-chosen options first.
Marketing before help ('Welcome to India's most trusted...'): callers want their option; keep the brand line to a few words.
Hold loops that repeat 'Your call is important to us': give estimated wait or queue position, offer a call-back, rotate genuinely useful messages.
Writing for the eye (abbreviations, 'w.e.f.', URLs with symbols): spell everything the way the voice artist or TTS must say it.

sources.title: Exotel: IVR scripts and prompts (2018-09-12)
sources.supports: keep scripts to 4-5 options; no more than three levels of menus; most-selected options first; prompts 15-30 seconds read aloud; write for the ear; state numbers slowly; language menu first; option to repeat the menu; keep messages updated; give estimated wait times; call-back option; avoid jargon and needless repetition of 'please' or 'dial'; inform callers that calls are recorded

sources.title: Holdcom: on-hold and IVR script samples
sources.supports: vendor selling scripted, voiced on-hold and IVR messages

cards.value_why: Low: on-hold and IVR vendors sell scripted, voiced messages (Holdcom) and Indian telephony vendors publish free script libraries (Exotel), so scripts are usually bundled with the voice and telephony service.
cards.goal: Reach the right department or answer in the fewest key presses, and stay on hold rather than hang up.

structure.does: Brand name, one-line purpose, call-recording notice if calls are recorded
First, before any menu; each language offered in its own language ('Hindi ke liye 1 dabaiye. For English, press 2.')
4-5 options, most-used first, one fixed pattern ('For order status, press 1'), repeat option last
Same pattern; never more than three levels deep
Estimated wait or queue position, call-back offer, 2-4 rotating useful messages (self-service, timings, documents to keep ready)
Working hours (with time zone for callers outside India), what to do now (WhatsApp, website, emergency number)
What to leave and when they will be called back

length.note: Measured in seconds when read aloud: 15-30 seconds per prompt (Exotel). Total words depend on menu depth and how many languages are recorded.

checklist: Is the greeting under about 10 seconds read aloud?
Does every menu have 5 or fewer options and the tree 3 or fewer levels?
Are the most-used options first?
Does every option follow the same pattern?
Is there an option to repeat the menu?
If calls are recorded, does the greeting say so?
Do hold messages give wait time or queue position and a call-back option?
Does the after-hours greeting state the hours and an alternative channel?
Is every number, abbreviation and URL written the way the voice must say it?
In a multilingual menu, is each language offered in that language?
pitfalls: Scripts approved on paper and never read aloud: read every prompt with a timer and cut anything over 30 seconds.
Formal translated Hindi ('Kripya pratiksha karein, aapki call hamare liye mahatvapurn hai'): use the everyday Hindustani callers speak ('Kripya line par bane rahiye, hum jaldi aapse baat karenge').
Outdated messages (last season's offer, old timings): date-stamp the script, set a review date, and update before every holiday.
'Please' and 'press' in every line: Exotel advises against needless repetition; one 'please' in the greeting is enough.
cards.exemplar_brief: IVR and on-hold script for a Patna multispeciality hospital's appointment line: Hindi first, English second; greeting with call-recording notice, language menu, a 5-option main menu (appointments, reports, emergency, insurance/TPA, other), one sub-menu for appointments, 3 rotating hold messages with a call-back offer, and an after-hours greeting; everyday Hindustani, not formal Hindi; 250-400 words; every prompt 30 seconds or less read aloud.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. Every brief part present and timed (greeting+recording notice 12 s, language menu offered in each language, 5-option menu with repeat, appointment sub-menu, 3 rotating hold messages with call-back on 9, after-hours with 112), numbers written as spoken. Misses: 'आपातकाल' (x3) is the formal Hindi the brief bans; Patna callers say 'इमरजेंसी'. Emergency is option 3 after the language menu; a hospital line should give the emergency route in the greeting. English 'to keep our service good' is awkward. Writer faults.

cards.name: Jingle / ad lyrics
cards.summary: A short sung brand line or song, from a few-second sonic logo to a one-minute ad song, written to be remembered and hummed. The writer delivers the hook line that carries the brand name or promise, lyrics that sit on a singable rhythm with syllables and stresses marked for the composer, and enough repetition to stick, in the language the audience actually sings in.
use_for: Ad songs for YouTube and Reels
Local business jingles (jewellers, sweet shops, coaching institutes)
Civic awareness and campaign songs (with the right compliance)
avoid: Cramming features into the lyric: a jingle sings one promise and the brand name; offers, prices and phone numbers go in spoken VO around it.
Lyrics with no rhythm: mark syllables and stresses per line, or write to the composer's guide tune, so the words sit on the beat.
Forced rhymes that twist Hindi word order ('chamakta hai jo, wahi lena tum'): rewrite the line or use assonance instead.
Spoken radio ads are genre:radio_spot_script; a line without music is genre:tagline_slogan.

cards.goal: Remember and hum the brand line days later and connect it to the brand name.

structure.does: Brand name plus promise in a short singable phrase that can stand alone as the mnemonic
A situation or benefit in the listener's world
The hook line repeated with small variation
Offer, address, phone or date in spoken VO, not sung
The hook line once more, brand name last

length.note: Set by duration: a sonic logo is one line, a 30-second radio jingle a few short sung verses plus chorus, a 60-second ad song longer; count against a sung read-through, not on paper.

checklist: Does the hook line contain the brand name or its promise?
Is the hook repeated at least twice?
Are syllable counts marked for lines sung to the same melody, and do they match?
Does the brand name land on a stressed beat or at a line end?
Is there only one promise in the sung lyric?
Are offers, phone numbers and addresses moved to spoken VO?
Do rhymes keep natural word order in the language used?
Is every claim one the brand can substantiate?
pitfalls: Lyrics translated from an English brief: write directly in the language people sing in (Hindi, Bhojpuri, Marathi) with everyday words.
A brand name that doesn't fit the metre: shape the melody line around the name; never mangle the name to fit.
Borrowing a film song's tune or a famous lyric line: that needs licensing; write an original line and give the composer a feel reference only.
Political or election jingles broadcast without the required pre-certification and labelling: check comp:eci_mcc first.
cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second radio jingle for a 40-year-old Varanasi sweet shop's Diwali gift boxes (Rs 499-1,999, free delivery within the city); audience: families across Varanasi; Hindi with a light Bhojpuri flavour; 40-70 sung words with a hook line of 6-8 syllables containing the shop's name, chorus sung 3 times, and an 8-10-second spoken insert for the price range (Rs 499 to Rs 1,999), free delivery within the city and the 10-digit phone number 98765 00000 (demo); syllable counts marked per line.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. The hook 'CHA-lis BA-ras ka KA-shi BHOG' (8 syllables, scans) carries both differentiators round 1 missed, 40 years and Kashi, with the name on the stressed line end; 'Ghat pe diya' places it in Varanasi; Bhog/log rhymes in natural word order; 'Diwali ba, Kashi Bhog ba' is a light, real Bhojpuri touch; every line counted at 8; 49 sung words; price range, free city delivery and the phone number in a 9-second spoken insert; the timing sums to 30 s. Nit (writer): 'mithaas se jud jaayein sab log' is the one generic line. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Job description / job post
cards.summary: A role description that attracts the right applicants and filters out the wrong ones: the job title people search, why the role exists, what success looks like in the first year, must-haves kept separate from nice-to-haves, pay band and work mode where possible, and exactly how to apply. Good JDs are specific, honest about the hard parts, and free of gendered, age-coded or exclusionary wording.
avoid: Creative titles ('Growth Ninja', 'Content Rockstar'): use the title people search ('Performance Marketing Manager') so the post is found.
A wish list of 15 'requirements': keep 3-6 true must-haves and label the rest as nice-to-have, so candidates can tell what really matters.
Age, gender or appearance coding ('young and dynamic', 'he will', 'male candidates preferred'): describe the work and the skills, not the person.
Hiding pay and work mode ('best in industry', 'as per norms'): state a band and onsite, hybrid or remote with the city, where the company allows.
Employer-brand campaigns and careers-page copy are genre:recruitment_ad.

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Job Description Writing
sources.supports: dedicated category on the Writing & Translation menu (seen 2026-10-04)

cards.value_why: Medium: Fiverr runs a dedicated Job Description Writing category on its Writing & Translation menu (seen 2026-10-04); most JDs are still written by hiring managers and HR, with paid work in bulk JD libraries and employer-branding projects.
cards.goal: The right candidates apply through the stated process, and the wrong ones self-select out.

structure.does: Searchable title, location and work mode, employment type, experience band, pay band
The problem this hire solves and who they work with
Responsibilities starting with verbs, in order of time spent
Outcomes at about 3, 6 and 12 months
Requirements truly needed on day one
Bonus skills, labelled optional
Pay band, real benefits (insurance, leave, learning budget), growth path
Stage, size and what the company does, honestly

structure.part: How to apply and the process
structure.does: What to send, the steps, the timeline, an equal-opportunity line

length.note: Senior and specialist roles need more context; job boards and mobile reading push toward 400-600 words.

checklist: Is the title one people search, without slang ('ninja', 'rockstar')?
Are location, work mode and experience band in the first lines?
Is a pay band given, or the reason it isn't?
Are 3-6 must-haves separated from nice-to-haves?
Does it describe first-year outcomes, not only duties?
Is it free of age, gender, marital-status or appearance requirements unrelated to the job?
Do responsibilities start with verbs, with no 'any other duty as assigned'?
Does it say how to apply, what to send and how long the process takes?
pitfalls: Copy-pasting an old JD: duties drift from the real job; rewrite with the hiring manager answering 'What will this person have done in 12 months?'
Internal acronyms and tool names candidates can't decode: spell them out the first time.
'Immediate joiners only' and similar filters added by habit: keep only real constraints and say why.
Asking for personal data the stage doesn't need (photo, father's name, marital status): remove it; collect only what hiring needs and say how it is used.

cards.name: Katha / mythological story narration
cards.summary: Narration of a mythological story, folk tale or saint's life in the kathavachak tradition, for audio series, YouTube, devotional apps or live recitation. Good katha narration names its source text and tradition, tells the episode in a warm storyteller's voice (direct address, rhetorical questions, sensory scenes), keeps characters and events faithful to that source, frames added dialogue as retelling, and ends with a short moral drawn from the story's own events.
avoid: Presenting invented episodes, dialogue or 'facts' as scripture: name the source (Valmiki Ramayana, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, a named Purana, a regional oral version) and frame added dialogue as retelling.
Mixing versions without saying so: pick one source per episode, or say 'In Tulsidas's telling...' when you switch.
A sermon instead of a story: the moral comes from the events, in 2-4 lines at the end, not as a lecture throughout.
Mocking, sectarian or caste-demeaning framing of any character or community: retell with respect and flag sensitive episodes for review.
Aarti, bhajan, stuti and vrat-katha texts are genre:devotional_content; an original fiction drama is genre:audio_series_script.

cards.goal: Listen to the end (and to the next episode), feel the story, and carry its moral into daily life.

structure.does: A short greeting or invocation suited to the tradition, then the hook: a question or a glimpse of the most dramatic moment ahead
Which text or tradition, where this episode sits in the larger story, who the characters are
Scenes in order with sensory detail, dialogue framed as retelling, rhetorical questions to the listener ('Sochiye, us samay Shabari ke man mein kya chal raha hoga?')
The test, choice or grace the episode turns on, told slowly
What the story teaches, tied to everyday life
Blessing or jaikara suited to the tradition, plus a tease for the next episode in a series

length.note: Set by format: a Shorts katha runs about a minute, an audio-series or YouTube episode several minutes, a live recitation far longer; time a read-aloud at the narrator's own pace rather than trusting a words-per-minute rule.

checklist: Is the source text or tradition named in the episode?
Are events and characters faithful to that source, with added dialogue framed as retelling?
Does the opening hook the listener within the first 30 seconds?
Does the narrator address the listener directly several times (questions, 'aap')?
Are key scenes told with sensory detail rather than summary?
Is the moral 2-4 lines, drawn from the story's events, at the end?
Are names and any shloka or chaupai spelled correctly in Devanagari (with IAST if romanised) and explained once?
Is there nothing mocking or demeaning toward any deity, community or caste?
In a series, does the episode end with a tease for the next one?
pitfalls: Sanskritised Hindi listeners can't follow by ear: narrate in spoken Hindustani and keep Sanskrit for names, shlokas and key terms, each explained once.
TTS mispronouncing names (Kaikeyi, Dashrath, Shabari): write names the way they must be spoken and test the voice before recording a whole series.
Cliffhangers built on invented twists: suspense must come from the real story's turns.
AI-generated visuals or voice presented as real in a katha video: YouTube requires creators to disclose realistic altered or synthetic content; label it.

cards.exemplar_brief: Katha narration script for a Hindi devotional YouTube channel: the story of Shabari's wait for Shri Ram, told from the Aranya Kand of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas; audience: Hindi-speaking families, many of them elderly listeners in UP and Bihar; spoken Hindustani in Devanagari with one chaupai quoted and explained; about 6-8 minutes read aloud (roughly 800-1,100 words); warm kathavachak voice with rhetorical questions; ends with a 3-line moral and a tease for the next episode.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Faithful to Manas Aranya Kand (Kabandha -> ashram, muni's words recalled, the lotus-eyed description, feet washed, kand-mool-phal eaten 'baarambaar bakhaani', 'adham' self-abasement, chaupai 'कह रघुपति सुनु भामिनि बाता। मानउँ एक भगति कर नाता॥' correct and explained, cloud-without-water simile, first two of the nine bhaktis, Pampa/Sugriva, yogic fire). Path-sweeping, Matang's line and the berry tale are clearly marked lok-parampara, not Tulsidas. Warm spoken Hindustani with rhetorical questions; 'उन्होंने फल नहीं खाए, उन्होंने बरसों की प्रतीक्षा खाई' is a line a kathavachak would keep. 3-line moral, tease (Hanuman in brahmin guise), jaikara. Nit: 'गुन' missing from the jaati-paanti list.
